summary: AE + SE walked Nova Commerce team through Redwood SDKs for Python and TypeScript, auth options (API key, SSO), environment setup, and quickstart examples. Discussed integration patterns for hosted vs dedicated, basic retry/backoff, and how Console and Optimize surfaces config suggestions. Agreed on POC next steps and to share security docs and example repos.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-10-20
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~10 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Sasha Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Nova CTO), Lucas Rivera (Lead Eng), Priya Singh (DevOps), Omar Diaz (PM)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood, i'm joined by Sasha, our solutions engineer. quick intro?
[00:08] Maya: hi, maya here, thanks, excited to see the SDK walkthrough, we're evaluating for chat and rerank flows.
[00:13] Sasha: awesome, we'll cover python and typescript quickstarts, auth patterns, and demo a small app on the console. if at any point stop me, ask questions.
[00:21] Lucas: cool, we care about latency and cost, also wanting to run in our VPC later.
[00:28] Jordan: noted. quick context question — current stack?
[00:31] Lucas: mostly node services, a small python microservice for ingestion, k8s on GCP, using OpenAI for prototyping.
[00:39] Sasha: great, so we'll show both SDKs. first — install steps are pip install redwood-inference and npm install @redwood/inference, quick and small. set REDWOOD_API_KEY or use SSO via our console.
[00:52] Maya: sso? we use Okta.
[00:54] Sasha: yep we support SAML/Okta — through the Console you can enable SSO and map groups to RBAC roles. for the SDK auth, for server-to-server the simplest is API key in env var; for user-initiated access we recommend short-lived tokens minted via our control plane tied to SSO sessions.
[01:10] Priya: any guidance on secret rotation and KMS?
[01:14] Sasha: we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for Private deployments; for Hosted we provide managed keys but you can also bring-your-own KMS via our Dedicated/Private offering. i'll share the exact docs after.
[01:25] Jordan: moving to the code demo — i'll share my screen.
[01:30] [screen share starts]
[01:33] Sasha: starting with Python quickstart: create a venv, pip install redwood-inference, export REDWOOD_API_KEY=pk_live_xxx, then simple snippet: client = RedwoodClient(); resp = client.chat.create({"model":"redwood-1.0","input":"hello"}) — you get JSON response, streaming is supported via client.chat.stream.
[01:55] Lucas: how do we handle streaming in node?
[01:58] Sasha: in TypeScript you can use client.chat.stream and hooks into async iterators, or the SDK exposes event callbacks. we'll paste the sample implementation in the repo.
[02:09] Maya: are there any gotchas with long context/kv cache?
[02:12] Sasha: good question — runtime manages KV cache, but if you do multiple replicas or edge routing you need to be aware of cache affinity. for most setups it's transparent; for dedicated low-latency workloads we have recommendations to pin sessions and share KV where appropriate.
[02:27] Jordan: briefly on env setup — we recommend keeping API keys in secret manager and injecting into pods as env vars, avoid checking them into repo. also we set REDWOOD_DEFAULT_MODEL in env to control model variant.
[02:40] Omar: whats the recommended retry/backoff logic?
[02:42] Sasha: standard exponential backoff with jitter; SDK includes a retry helper that retries idempotent calls. for streaming we recommend reconnect logic and checkpointing token offsets.
[02:55] Lucas: ok. what about sample rates for logging and cost visibility?
[02:58] Jordan: Console gives per-route token cost breakdowns and sample request logging; for PII we mask via built-in redactions or customers can use local pre-send filters.
[03:12] Maya: show us the Console quickstart.
[03:15] [screen] Sasha: opening Console — you can create an API key, configure route-level policies, and enable Optimize suggestions. the Optimize tab surfaces batching and quantization recommendations based on historical token patterns — it's not magic but it's helpful to reduce unit costs.
[03:36] Priya: what's required for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[03:39] Sasha: Dedicated is reserved capacity on GPUs in your cloud region, gives you fixed throughput and private tenancy. Hosted is our managed multi-tenant API. Private (VPC) option gives a customer-managed network and optional on-prem packaging. for compliance, Private supports bringing your KMS and audit logs.
[03:58] Lucas: timeline — we want to run a POC in staging in 1 week. is that feasible?
[04:02] Jordan: yes, we often spin up a POC workspace and provide test credits. we'll share a quickstart repo and a staging checklist.
[04:10] Maya: any sample metrics we should collect?
[04:12] Sasha: collect p95 latency, tokens per request, success/error rates, and quality metrics (we can provide evaluation harness).
[04:20] Jordan: switching to auth deep-dive — here's example of using Okta SAML: you configure SAML provider in Console, map groups to roles, then you can generate short-lived tokens for SDKs via redirect or service flow.
[04:36] Priya: for our CI pipelines, we prefer service accounts — how would that look?
[04:39] Sasha: create service account in Console, generate key, store in secret manager, rotate keys periodically. for extra security in Private, you can configure mutual TLS between our control plane and your network.
[04:52] Lucas: anything on network egress and data residency?
[04:55] Sasha: we have region controls for Hosted and Dedicated; with Private, you control egress. we'll share our data residency whitepaper.
[05:05] Maya: can we use our own model variants or do we have to use Redwood-managed?
[05:09] Sasha: you can bring your own model in Dedicated/Private, or use our curated catalog in Hosted. model pinning and rollout is supported.
[05:18] Lucas: switching back to SDK specifics — do you have TypeScript typings and is there support for deno?
[05:23] Sasha: TS typings are first-class; deno isn't officially supported yet but the SDK is lightweight so many teams get it working. we'll add notes in the repo.
[05:32] Jordan: variable naming and config — we recommend REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_DEFAULT_MODEL, REDWOOD_BASE_URL for self-hosted endpoints.
[05:44] Maya: how does billing and cost attribution work?
[05:46] Jordan: Console provides cost per route and you can tag keys for teams — for Dedicated we provide a monthly commit and usage reports.
[05:56] Lucas: okay. show us an example of calling embeddings from python.
[05:59] Sasha: sure — from redwood_inference import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(); emb = client.embeddings.create({"model":"embed-1.0","input": ["text1","text2"]}) — returns vectors. we'll include a notebook.
[06:18] Omar: how to handle schema validation for structured outputs?
[06:21] Sasha: SDK supports function calling and structured output validation hooks; plus you can include JSON schema validation client-side.
[06:30] Jordan: quick note on error modes — for latency-critical flows use fallback models, circuit breakers, and progressive backoff. the SDK supports automatic fallbacks configured in route policies.
[06:45] Maya: any recommended quantization for lower-cost inference?
[06:48] Sasha: Optimize will propose quant profiles based on your workload; generally int8 quant works well for embeddings-heavy workloads, but for chat you might pick 4-bit or mixed precision. we'll share guidance.
[07:00] Lucas: can we run local benchmarks?
[07:03] Sasha: yes, we provide a benchmark script in the repo that hits the same endpoints and measures p50/p95/p99. for Dedicated you can run on the same instance type to get realistic numbers.
[07:18] Maya: what's the onboarding time for infra?
[07:21] Jordan: for basic Hosted POC it's hours to a day; Dedicated takes longer for procurement and capacity, typically weeks. Private is longest due to network and compliance.
[07:34] Lucas: any security concerns around logs? we need to keep PII out.
[07:38] Sasha: Console can redact fields and we have routing rules to avoid logging sensitive paths. also audit logs and access logs are available for compliance.
[07:49] Maya: fine. demo time — please run the quickstart app.
[07:52] Sasha: starting the node quickstart: npm run start, env vars set, connecting to Redwood Hosted endpoint via REDWOOD_API_KEY, spin up chat session, streaming messages show up. there's a small spinner as messages come in.
[08:12] Lucas: looks good. how hard to swap provider?
[08:15] Sasha: if you abstract client calls and env vars, it's straightforward. but our SDK has convenience helpers for batching and streaming that others may not.
[08:26] Omar: do you have middleware for request-level auth?
[08:29] Sasha: yes, we provide express/fastify middleware for token validation and request attribution.
[08:38] Maya: what about rate limits?
[08:40] Jordan: Hosted has per-key rate limits; Dedicated you can configure throughput. Console shows rate limit usage and can alert.
[08:55] Lucas: ok moving to questions from our engineering team — Priya: about CI/CD and terraform?
[08:59] Priya: we manage infra with terraform, can Redwood be managed programmatically?
[09:03] Sasha: yes, we have terraform modules and an API for programmatic config — we'll share examples.
[09:10] Jordan: quick callouts on best practices: use short-lived tokens for user flows, pin models for regression safety, instrument token-level metrics.
[09:20] Maya: excellent. any mention of competitors?
[09:22] Jordan: customers often evaluate OpenAI and Anthropic; some teams look at Replicate for self-hosting. key diffs are runtime performance, cost controls, and deployment flexibility.
[09:34] Lucas: cost controls — is there automatic batching?
[09:36] Sasha: yes, SDK and runtime support automatic batching; Optimize suggests batch sizes and cache policies from historical patterns.
[09:46] Jordan: wrapping up — recap and next steps. we'll send the quickstart repo, security docs, and a staging checklist. Nova to spin up staging and run our benchmark script. schedule follow-up for 2026-10-27.
[09:59] Maya: thanks, that works.
[10:02] Jordan: thanks everyone, end of demo.

Notes: transcription contains a few ASR artifacts; some product names abbreviated. shared resources mentioned: https://github.com/redwood-inference/quickstarts, Security whitepaper link (will be shared by Sasha).
